title: Joy to wrestle (Tanya 26)
hook: a sluggish wrestler can't win; sadness weighs down service
tomorrow: a verse says the wicked just vanishes. why did a rebbe hear hope?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tanya's title page: the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart. Very near to you. Today, the thing that slows you down on the way to it.

Third period of a high school wrestling match, and the bigger kid is losing. He should win. He's stronger, heavier, been on the mat longer. But he's been off since the whistle: shoulders down, a beat late on every move. The smaller kid isn't stronger. He's just quick, and he looks like he's having fun out there. Coaches have a word for what's wrong with the bigger kid. So does a book of Jewish teaching, and it uses a wrestling match too. So who wins when strength shows up heavy?
screen: `THIRD PERIOD. THE BIG KID IS LOSING.` → `A BEAT LATE ON EVERY MOVE.` → `WHO WINS WHEN STRENGTH SHOWS UP HEAVY?`

segments.voice: The book is the Tanya, by the Chabad teacher Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi. In chapter twenty-six he sets up the same match. Two people wrestle. One is lazy and sluggish, and he'll be thrown easily, even if he's the stronger one. So it is, he says, with the struggle inside a person against the pull toward wrong. You can't win it heavy. The heaviness he means comes from sadness, the flat, low kind that makes everything feel pointless. What wins is quickness, and quickness comes from joy. That's the surprise. Joy isn't the prize at the end of the struggle. It's the grip you need to start it. The Psalms have the old line for it: Serve the LORD with gladness. The Tanya isn't asking anyone to fake a smile, and it isn't waving away real grief. Regret has its place, it says, at its own set time, the way you'd plan a hard conversation instead of having it all day long. What it warns against is letting the low mood run the whole match. Its word for that mood is atzvut, a heavy sadness. And the opposite, simchah, joy, is more than a feeling here. It's a way of moving: lighter on your feet, first to the next move. Back to the gym. The smaller kid isn't winning because nothing's hard. He's winning because he came to wrestle glad.
screen: `TWO WRESTLERS, ONE SLUGGISH.` · `HEAVINESS COMES FROM SADNESS.` · `JOY IS THE GRIP, NOT THE PRIZE.` · `REGRET GETS ITS OWN TIME.` · then, large: `JOY TO WRESTLE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, or sit tall where you are. Shake out your hands, then your shoulders, for a few seconds, the way a wrestler loosens up before stepping onto the mat, then let yourself go still with your feet planted. Bring to mind one thing you've been dragging your feet on, and see yourself taking the first step toward it lightly, quick and glad.
screen: `SHAKE IT OUT.` · `FEET PLANTED.` · `ONE THING, TAKEN LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Joy to wrestle: the Tanya's picture of the inner struggle. Sadness makes a person sluggish; joy makes them quick enough to win.
For the road: joy to wrestle, because heavy loses the match and glad gets the first move. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Tanya is a central text of Chabad Hasidism, studied in classes and in a daily study cycle; its call to serve God with joy rather than heaviness is a frequent theme at Hasidic gatherings, where songs are sung to lift the mood.

Tanya.meaning: a Hasidic book of teaching on the inner life

Chabad.meaning: a Hasidic movement whose central text is the Tanya

Schneur Zalman of Liadi.meaning: the rabbi who wrote the Tanya

atzvut.meaning: a heavy sadness that makes a person sluggish

sources.ref: Tanya, Likutei Amarim, chapter 26 (two wrestlers: the lazy and sluggish one is easily thrown even if stronger; so too sadness and heaviness hinder the struggle with the evil inclination; joy brings alacrity)

notes: Tanya ch. 26 paraphrased: the wrestler parable; sadness/heaviness vs. joy and alacrity. 'Regret has its place, at its own set time' summarizes the chapter's point that even sadness over sins belongs at an appropriate set time, not during service; confirm it is ch. 26 (and not only ch. 31, which distinguishes bitterness from sadness).
Psalm 100:2 quoted from JPS 1917 ('Serve the LORD with gladness'); the lesson does not claim the Tanya cites this verse in ch. 26. Confirm wording.
'Chabad teacher' used instead of 'founder of Chabad' under the claims rule. howItsDone mentions a daily study cycle and joy as a theme at Hasidic gatherings (farbrengens); confirm framing.
Shape story: the hook is a wrestling match already under way, its question answered by the teach. Practice kind: body posture / movement (shake out, then stand still).
